title: Epistemic Pairwise Maximin Share
claim: Our new notion sits in a web of implications and non-implications among existing fairness notions, which this map makes precise.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right DAGs of boxes, gray crossed arrows mark non-implications
description: Two stacked panels of boxed fairness-notion names joined by arrows, all in black and white. Panel (a) is a left-to-right directed graph. GMMS on the far left branches to PMMS and EGMMS. These lead to EFX, EPMMS, EEFX and MMS, and the graph ends at 4/7-MMS on the right. EPMMS sits in the center. Two gray double-headed arrows with an X show that EPMMS is not equivalent to EFX or to MMS. Panel (b) is a smaller graph: PMMS points to EFX and to IMMP, MMS points to IMMP, IMMP points to IMMX, EFX points to IMMX, and IMMX points to 4/7-MMS. Sub-captions sit below each panel. There is no color, and the eye goes to the central EPMMS node and the crossed gray arrows.
caption: Implications between fairness notions under non-degenerate additive valuations. Most implications follow directly from the definitions; the following require proof: (1) PMMS ⇒EFX and EPMMS ⇒EEFX on non-degenerate instances [23]; (2) MMS ⇒EEFX [24]; and (3) EEFX and IMMX ⇒4/7-MMS [8]. In Appendix A.3, we show that EPMMS is incomparable to both MMS and EFX.
abstract: We introduce epistemic pairwise maximin share (EPMMS), a new fairness notion for fair division of indivisible goods. Two fundamental notions in this setting are envy-freeness up to any item (EFX) and pairwise maximin share (PMMS), with PMMS being stronger than EFX. While EFX has been extensively studied, far less is known about PMMS. Recent work shows that relaxing EFX via an epistemic perspective leads to substantial progress on the EFX problem, raising the question of whether a similar approach can advance our understanding of PMMS. Motivated by this, we initiate the study of EPMMS, the epistemic relaxation of PMMS. EPMMS is more challenging than EEFX: the key approaches underlying recent progress on epistemic EFX inherently fail to extend to EPMMS. We establish the following results. (1) For additive valuations, $4/5$-EPMMS allocations exist and can be efficiently computed. (2) For bivalued valuations, EPMMS allocations exist and can be efficiently computed; in fact, we obtain the stronger guarantee of epistemic groupwise maximin share (EGMMS), which also strengthens the existence of MMS allocations for this setting. (3) We prove that EPMMS allocations exist in two settings where MMS allocations need not exist: instances with three additive agents or two types of additive agents.
